subject: anaesthesia
title: Neonatal anaesthesia and physiology: transition and hernias

steps.tx: At birth **fetal haemoglobin** holds oxygen tightly with a left shifted curve, and pulmonary resistance falls as the lungs expand. Rising oxygen closes the **ductus arteriosus**, while prostaglandin keeps it open when the heart depends on it. Glucose **under 45** needs treatment, and temperature control near **36.5** with servo control and humidity protects the baby. Caffeine treats apnoea in the preterm baby during this transition.
steps.say: Fetal blood holds oxygen more tightly than adult blood after birth. Breathing expands the lungs and lowers the resistance inside their blood vessels. Rising oxygen then closes the fetal channel between the great arteries naturally. Low blood sugar and low body temperature can both harm the newborn brain quickly. A stimulant medicine supports breathing while the preterm baby adapts to life.

steps.tx: This colour Doppler echo shows a **patent ductus arteriosus** with a left to right shunt between the aorta and pulmonary arteries. The inset contrasts **prostaglandin**, which keeps the duct open, with **indomethacin**, which helps to close it. The image matters because duct direction decides treatment in duct dependent heart disease. For the exam, read the colour jet as flow crossing from the aorta into the pulmonary circuit.
steps.say: The ultrasound uses colour to show blood crossing through a fetal channel that stayed open. Red and yellow flow will move from the body artery toward the lung artery. A small heart diagram will label two drugs that push the channel in opposite directions. One drug preserves the channel when the heart depends on its flow. The other drug will encourage closure when the open channel harms the baby.

vis.alt: Color Doppler echo showing ductal shunt between aorta and pulmonary arteries with heart inset.
vis.caption: Doppler echo showing patent ductus arteriosus shunt. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Suxamethonium** can slow the neonatal heart, so atropine stays ready, while rocuronium with sugammadex suits selected cases. **Sevoflurane** remains the usual induction choice, and caudal or spinal blocks reduce opioid needs after surgery. The airway uses a straight **Miller** blade of size 0 or 1 with an uncuffed tube. Ex preterm babies need apnoea monitoring for **12 hours** after anaesthesia.
steps.say: Some muscle relaxants slow the newborn heart and need an antidote drug ready nearby. An inhaled agent usually induces anaesthesia smoothly in this small age group. Blocks near the spine provide pain relief and reduce the need for strong opioids. A straight blade lifts the floppy epiglottis directly during tube placement in babies. Former preterm babies need breathing observation for many hours after surgery.

steps.tx: In **tracheoesophageal fistula** the mother may have excess fluid in pregnancy, and the tube coils in the upper pouch on film, as this diagram shows. The baby stays upright to limit aspiration, and nitrous oxide stays avoided because it distends bowel. **Inguinal hernia** repair in an ex preterm baby may use an awake spinal to cut apnoea risk. Necrotising bowel disease may need a stoma and intravenous nutrition.
steps.say: The diagram can show the common patterns where the food pipe ends blindly or joins the airway. A feeding tube curls back inside the blind upper pouch on the chest film. Keeping the baby upright reduces milk spilling into the lungs through the abnormal connection. Certain gases expand trapped bowel and stay avoided during the repair operation. Awake spinal anaesthesia can reduce breathing pauses after hernia repair in ex preterm babies.

vis.alt: Diagram showing common types of tracheoesophageal fistula and esophageal atresia, including a chest X-ray with a coiled nasogastric tube in the upper esophageal pouch.
vis.caption: Common types of tracheoesophageal fistula and esophageal atresia

steps.tx: The **PIPP** score grades neonatal pain from facial and physiologic signs, and **sucrose** with a pacifier soothes brief procedures. Caudal and spinal blocks plus scheduled **paracetamol** reduce opioid exposure after surgery. Transport uses a warm incubator with secure lines and a structured **SBAR** handoff to the receiving team. Follow up screens vision, hearing and growth after discharge from the unit.
steps.say: A validated score helps the team judge pain in a baby who cannot speak. Sweet solution on a dummy calms the baby during short painful procedures. Regional blocks and regular simple analgesia reduce the need for strong opioids afterward. Warm transport with secure lines protects the baby between units during transfer. Structured handover and later screening complete safe neonatal surgical care.
